title: Roving Tabindex & Composite Widgets 🎮
description: Master the roving tabindex pattern for menus, toolbars, and grids to optimize keyboard navigation.

slides.title: The Problem: Tab Through Every Item? 😩
slides.content:
In a list of menu items, tabs, or a toolbar, you don't want the user to have to press Tab 20 times to get through all items. That's tedious.

Solution: **Roving tabindex**.

- Only one item in the group is focusable (tabindex="0").
- All other items have tabindex="-1".
- The user presses Tab to reach the group (focuses the single active item).
- Then arrow keys move focus among the items, updating tabindex dynamically.

This makes the group behave like a single tab stop.

quizData.question: In a roving tabindex menu, how many items have `tabindex="0"` at any time?
quizData.explanation: Only the currently focused item gets tabindex="0"; others are tabindex="-1".

slides.title: Implementing Roving Tabindex 🛠️
slides.content:
Steps:

1. Initialize the widget: set tabindex="0" on the first item, "-1" on others.
2. Attach keydown listener to the container (or each item) for Arrow keys.
3. On arrow key:
   - Set current item's tabindex="-1".
   - Move focus to next/prev item (using index math).
   - Set its tabindex="0" and call `focus()` on it.

This pattern is used in tabs (Chapter 5), menus, toolbars, listboxes, and grids.

quizData.question: What key event should you listen for to move focus between items in a roving tabindex menu?
quizData.explanation: Arrow keys move focus inside the widget; Tab moves focus out to the next tab stop.

slides.title: When to Use Roving Tabindex vs. Tab Stops 🤔
slides.content:
- Use roving tabindex when the group should be treated as a single tab stop (menus, toolbars, tab lists, radio groups).
- Use individual tab stops (all items focusable) when each item needs to be directly reachable by Tab – like a list of links where each is distinct.

The ARIA Authoring Practices guide provides patterns for each widget.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Simplify with `aria-activedescendant`
For complex widgets like listboxes, you can keep focus on the container and use `aria-activedescendant` to point to the active item without moving DOM focus. Useful for virtual scrolling.
